where: Section 1 (amplitude sentence and joint-state formula), Section 3 (probability line and the two-register kickback formula), Quiz Q1 (formula and amplitude)
problem: The normalisation factor is written as 1/√(2n), which equals 1/√(2·n), not the required 1/√(2ⁿ). The state formula at the top of Section 1 correctly uses 2<sup>n</sup>, but every later occurrence drops the superscript, and the line |±1/√(2n)|² = 1/2ⁿ is then self-contradictory. A student copying 1/√(2n) would get a non-normalised state and a wrong amplitude for every input string.
fix: Use 1/√(2ⁿ) everywhere: each input has amplitude 1/√(2ⁿ); the joint state is (1/√(2ⁿ)) Σx |x⟩|f(x)⟩; the kickback state is (1/√(2ⁿ)) Σx (−1)^f(x) |x⟩|−⟩; the measurement probability is |±1/√(2ⁿ)|² = 1/2ⁿ. Quiz Q1: H⊗n|0ⁿ⟩ = (1/√(2ⁿ)) Σx |x⟩, each of the 2ⁿ strings with amplitude 1/√(2ⁿ).

problem: "Uf is its own inverse and therefore unitary" is a false implication: plenty of maps are self-inverse and not unitary, and being involutive says nothing about preserving inner products. The reversibility argument and the unitarity argument are being merged into one wrong step.
fix: Because y ⊕ f(x) ⊕ f(x) = y, applying Uf twice returns the input, so Uf is its own inverse and the computation is reversible. Separately, Uf maps each computational basis state |x⟩|y⟩ to another basis state |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩ and never merges two basis states, so it is a permutation of the basis; a permutation matrix is unitary, hence Uf is a valid quantum gate. (It is also Hermitian, since Uf = Uf⁻¹.)

where: Section 3, global versus relative phase paragraph
problem: "Kickback always makes the second kind, one sign per input" is not true when f is constant: then every sign is the same and the result is a global phase, exactly the case Quiz Q6 describes. The absolute "always" clashes with Q6.
fix: Kickback gives a relative phase whenever f takes both values 0 and 1, since then the signs differ between basis states; if f is constant, all signs are equal and the factor is global and unobservable, which is why constant versus balanced needs interference to be distinguished.
